en: The Thousand-Character Classic in Sanskrit, with Preface, appended to the work composed by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing.

This preface to the *Sanskrit Thousand-Character Classic* was written for the purpose of providing a model for linguistic study for people in the Western Regions; it includes transliterated equivalents in both Chinese and Sanskrit, with the titles inscribed below each section.

As for Chinese characters that lack corresponding [Sanskrit] words, they are corrected by means of their phonetic values; these are all essential characters for the current path. If one masters these, all other terminology will be understood. This differs from the traditional *Qianziwen* (Thousand Character Classic); if one studies it alongside the Siddham chapters, one will be capable of translating Sanskrit texts within one or two years.

This is the table of contents for the Thousand-Character Classic in Sanskrit.
It was transmitted by former sages as having been composed by the Tripitaka Master Yijing.
However, among the ancient records, citations of its literary content exist, yet the complete work has long remained hidden.

Formerly, while in Dongwu, I happened to transcribe a single copy from among the decayed slips remaining in a ruined basket; it was incomplete. Recently, while traveling in Luoyang, I fortunately obtained several other versions.

During my leisure from meditation, I have collated and verified them, roughly restoring the correct text. Having extensively researched the diverse accounts from the Indian lands, I have thoroughly washed away the lingering doubts regarding the sacred scriptures. Now that this precious secret is no longer kept hidden, I alone can unfold it with a smile.

Reflecting upon the author’s instruction of others and the universal reach of his benevolence, how could I possibly conceal my own failings? Thus, I have diligently perused the contents of this volume and engaged in its carving and engraving. Written on the full moon of the second month in the spring of the year Dingwei of the Jōhō era, by the Yuga-śramaṇa Jakumei while residing as a sojourner in Rakudō.

General Principles: First, this work is also titled *The Thousand-Character Classic of India and Tang (Fan-Tang Qianziwen)*. Anran’s record states that it was requested by Great Master Cijue; having now examined several extant copies and compared them with one another, errors remain. May scholars who peruse this work be fortunate enough to obtain a superior version and further verify its accuracy.

In some cases, the phonetic rhymes of the Chinese and Tang translations may not correspond; if one cannot verify this by consulting various editions and finds no basis for correction, one should leave it as it is without alteration. Even if there were clear textual evidence in the scriptures or manuals, the intention behind failing to rely on that to excise this [inconsistency] is evident.

First, regarding those passages where the various editions differ and are difficult to resolve abruptly, I have provided interlinear annotations and placed them at the beginning of the volume; furthermore, I have appended Chinese characters for the benefit of young students.
Second, there are two fragments of Central Indian palm-leaf manuscripts preserved at Hōryū-ji Temple in Wajō.
These are the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* and the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī*.
At the end, the fourteen vowels of the Siddham script appear.

Currently, the Sanskrit characters herein imitate those on palm-leaf manuscripts and are so intermingled with the calligraphic styles of the present age that they are difficult to distinguish; they have merely followed the conventions of the times.
Just as the second consonant of the labial class (oṣṭhya) is written in the form of 𑀓 (ka),

while the second consonant of the dental class (dantya) is written in the form of 𑀓 (ka)— the latter being omitted because it is difficult to model— so too is the second consonant of the palatal class (tālavya) written in the form of 𑀓 (ca).
The second guttural is written as 􄕣;
the fourth is written as 􈍡 and the fourth dot of the *mātrā* is written as 􈎿.
The seventh is written as 􆿏, and although the distinct *mātrā* forms 􈏀 and 􈏁 differ from the standard rules, they do not overlap; other minor variations can be seen by examining them.

In this present work, the four characters of each line form a rhyming couplet; yet it has been copied numerous times with errors, characters appear and disappear, and the arrangement is chaotic. Even after comparing several volumes, no consistent order can be found. Moreover, since it contrasts Chinese with Sanskrit, how could its underlying intent be clarified? Even if one were to compose verses in the manner of Xingsi’s "Matching Rhymes" (Xingsi ciyun), how could one possibly reconcile the linguistic nuances and meanings of two different nations?
